newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesian coffee crop seen down 15-20 pct - trade.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian coffee crop seen down 15-20 pct - trade.

text.p: Southeast Asian coffee dealers said on Wednesday they expected the fall in Indonesia's coffee output this year to be less dramatic than a 30 per percent cut in an original forecast made by a senior official this week.
Traders polled by Reuters estimated a decline in production, from earlier predictions, of between 15-20 percent in 1997.

Oesman Soedargo, chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters (AICE), said on Monday the coffee crop could be 30 percent short of an original forecast of 480,000 tonnes with exports reaching 220,000 tonnes against 300,000 tonnes in 1996.
"We think a reduction of 15-20 percent is realistic," a coffee dealer for a European commodity house told Reuters.
Another veteran coffee dealer for a Singapore-based trading company said he has some doubts about the extent of damage inflicted on Indonesia's coffee plantations by adverse weather.
"I think 30 percent is on the high side. I believe 20 percent is more likely," he said.
Traders said the total volume of Indonesia's 1997 coffee exports will probably reach between 250,000-270,000 tonnes, of which around 20,000-30,000 tonnes would be arabica beans and the rest robusta.

"That would mean that Indonesian exports will be equal to the Vietnamese crop," one trader said. "By next year, Vietnam's exports could easily reach 300,000 tonnes and they may soon overtake Indonesia as the top producer in Asia."

The dealers were divided, however, about the impact of a 20 percent fall in Indonesian output on coffee prices in the international market. Indonesia is the third biggest coffee producer in the world behind Brazil and Colombia.
One dealer said Indonesia's lower output may be negated by higher-than-expected coffee production in countries such as Vietnam, Uganda, and the Ivory Coast.
"That would compensate for any drop in the Indonesian crop," the dealer said.

But another trader said higher output in the Ivory Coast and Vietnam would not be sufficient to offset expected falls in Brazil and Indonesia given the larger production bases of these last two countries -- the leading producers of robusta coffee in the world.
"The shortfall will not be offset by any increase in production," he said.

Concern over the size of Brazil's 1997/98 crop, which is estimated to reach around 20-24 million 60 kg bags against 27 million in 1996/97, has been a major factor in the recent rally in international coffee prices.

Another dealer said the market also has to factor in the absence of Zaire, which exports about 60,000 tonnes of robusta beans a year and where a raging civil war has driven the country out of the coffee market.
"They sure as hell won't be exporting this year," he said.

More robusta beans are starting to reach the ports in Inbdonesia as the harvest gets underway, but there has been no build-up in stocks with most of the coffee quickly snapped up by buyers, traders said.
"There's quite good quantities coming in. A lot of coffee is committed already," one said.
Indonesia's benchmark Grade 4 coffee, 80 defects, was quoted by the trade at around US$1,350-$1,370 a tonne FOB Lampung compared with last week's $1,400-$1,500.
In Vietnam, the country's coffee harvest is largely over with the trade estimating that about 40,000 to 60,000 tonnes of robusta beans remain in warehouses in the country.
"Vietnam is almost over," a trader said, adding business in the country is now "very quiet."
The price of Vietnam's Grade 2 coffee, 8.0 percent black and broken, was seen by dealers at $1,340-$1,350 a tonne FOB Saigon against $1,350-$1,400 a tonne FOB on the same basis last week.
The London robusta coffee market is seen by regional coffee dealers opening unchanged to $10 lower in dull conditions.
"It's due $8-$10 lower just on pure numbers," one said.
Trading in the robusta coffee contract in the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) reached a meagre 21 lots on Tuesday.
Nine lots of the July contract ended at $1,455 a tonne, six lots of the September contract finished at $1,448 a tonne and the remaining six lots of the November contract closed at $1,445 a tonne.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
